HYPOTHESIS (final answer to: "In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?"):

Individuals with a criminal record (ever_jailed = 1) had significantly lower composite wealth than individuals without a criminal record in ALL THREE survey years — 1985, 1990, and 1996. In each year, the jailed group's median and mean wealth were lower, and the Mann-Whitney U test (two-sided, alpha = 0.05) rejected the null: 1985 p = 1.6e-10; 1990 p = 7.8e-35; 1996 p = 9.3e-26. Conclusions hold under Welch t-tests, Bonferroni correction, race×sex-stratified CMH tests, and after removing duplicate rows.

payload.hypothesis: Individuals with a criminal record (ever_jailed = 1) were found to have significantly lower composite wealth than individuals without a criminal record (ever_jailed = 0) in all three survey years: 1985 (Mann-Whitney U p = 1.6e-10; median wealth $720 vs $3,600), 1990 (p = 7.8e-35; $0 vs $10,500), and 1996 (p = 9.3e-26; $0 vs $8,500). The association is significant at alpha = 0.05 in every year and is robust to Welch t-tests, Bonferroni correction, race-by-sex stratification (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel), and removal of duplicate rows.
payload.workflow: Inspected data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; all documented columns present; no missing values; ever_jailed: 289 jailed vs 11,724 not; wealth in raw dollars, skewed with zeros and negatives). For each year (1985, 1990, 1996) compared composite wealth between ever_jailed=1 and ever_jailed=0 using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests at alpha=0.05 (primary), with Welch t-tests, Bonferroni-adjusted p-values (x3), and a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratified by race x sex as sensitivity checks; repeated the analysis on de-duplicated data (10,114 rows) to confirm robustness. All tests showed significantly lower wealth for the jailed group in all three years.
